common_name: Rocket Blast Daylily (Red Tetraploid with Green Throat)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions or potted fans in spring or early fall with the crown about an inch below the soil surface in full sun and well-drained, moderately fertile soil.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown set about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, watering regularly until new fans take hold. Hybridized by O. David Niswonger and registered in 2001, Rocket Blast carries bright red, lightly ruffled single flowers with a subtly deeper red eye zone over a green throat, held on well-branched 32-inch scapes. The cultivar won the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 2007, an honor voted on by convention attendees touring member gardens. Established, dormant-foliage clumps are vigorous rebloomers that benefit from division every three to four years to keep bud counts high.

common_name: Beautiful Edgings Daylily (Cream with Rose Picotee Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, spacing clumps to allow good air movement around the fragrant blooms.

directions: Set divisions in spring or early fall in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, giving each clump room to fill in over several seasons. Bred by Nita and Donald Copenhaver and registered in 1989, Beautiful Edgings opens cream-based single flowers edged in rose pink above a green throat on 30-inch scapes through a fragrant midseason bloom with some rebloom. It went on to win the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 2002 and the Lenington All-American Award in 2006, recognition reserved for cultivars that perform well across many regions. Diploid and semi-evergreen, it multiplies steadily and is best divided every few years once clumps become crowded.

common_name: South Sea Enchantment Daylily (Fragrant Rose Pink Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and humus-rich, well-drained soil, watering regularly while new fans establish.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and humus-rich, well-drained soil, keeping new plantings evenly moist until established. Hybridized by Oliver L. F. Billingslea and registered in 1996, this diploid carries fragrant, rose-pink self flowers with a green throat on compact 21-inch scapes, with an extended bloom habit that keeps individual flowers open later in the day than most cultivars. It earned the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 1999. Semi-evergreen and free-flowering through its midseason display, it clumps up readily and rewards division every few years.

common_name: Tuscawilla Princess Daylily (Pink Self with Olive Throat)

planting.note: Install divisions in spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil, keeping new plantings evenly watered until established.

directions: Install divisions in spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil, watering deeply until fans root in. Registered in 1990 by Ra Hansen, Tuscawilla Princess carries soft pink single flowers with a small olive-green throat on 26-inch scapes, with an extended bloom habit that lets individual flowers stay open later into the day. It was honored with the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 1996. Diploid and semi-evergreen, it is a dependable, floriferous midseason rebloomer distinct from the same hybridizer's later, larger-flowered 'Tuscawilla Tigress'.

common_name: In the Heart of It All Daylily (Rose Purple Tetraploid Self)
scientific_name: Hemerocallis 'In the Heart of It All'

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring with the crown just below the soil surface in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Plant divisions in spring with the crown just below the soil surface in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Hybridized by Elizabeth Salter and registered in 2005, it bears rose-purple single self flowers over a green throat on 28-inch scapes during an early-midseason bloom with dependable rebloom later in the year. The cultivar won the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 2005 and went on to receive the Society's Award of Merit in 2025. Tetraploid and dormant, it forms vigorous clumps that benefit from division every few years to sustain heavy bud counts.

common_name: Mary Alice Daylily (Pink with Raspberry Red Eye and Edge)

planting.note: Set divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, watering deeply while fans re-establish.

directions: Set divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, watering deeply while fans re-establish. Registered in 2007 from a cross of tetraploid 'Siloam Ralph Henry' and 'Cherry Valentine', Mary Alice produces clean baby-ribbon pink single flowers with a deep raspberry-red eye and matching picotee edge above a bright green throat on 34-inch scapes. The cultivar won the American Hemerocallis Society's President's Cup in 2009, an honor voted on by convention attendees touring member gardens. Tetraploid and semi-evergreen with reliable rebloom, it is best divided every three to four years as clumps become congested.

common_name: Gold Wool Clematis (Fuzzy Golden-Stemmed Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring with the root ball shaded and cool while the top is trained into full sun on a sturdy support.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring with the root ball shaded and cool while the top is trained into full sun on a sturdy support. Clematis chrysocoma, a close ally of the better-known C. montana, is native to Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou in China and is covered in soft golden-brown down along its young stems, leaf undersides and flower stalks. It opens single, saucer-shaped white to pale-pink flowers on old wood in late spring, slightly later in the season than most C. montana selections. Prune lightly right after flowering only if needed, since next year's buds form on the current season's growth.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below grade to keep roots cool, training young growth onto a trellis or through a shrub.

directions: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below grade to keep roots cool, training young growth onto a trellis or through a shrub in full sun to light shade. Native to high-elevation scrub across Gansu, Qinghai, Sichuan, Yunnan and West Nei Mongol in China, Clematis akebioides is closely related to the more commonly grown C. tangutica and C. orientalis but carries thicker, glaucous pinnate leaves and nodding, bell-shaped greenish-yellow flowers often stained red or purple on the outside of the sepals. Flowers appear from summer into fall and are followed by fluffy silvery seed heads that extend the display into winter. Because it blooms on new growth, cut it back hard in late winter to keep the vine tidy and encourage strong flowering.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

common_name: Marbled New Zealand Clematis (Dwarf Evergreen Alpine Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun and sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil, ideally in a raised bed, trough or rock garden.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun and sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil, ideally in a raised bed, trough or rock garden where the tufted, suckering growth can hug stone. Clematis marmoraria is endemic to marble karst outcrops in the mountains of northwest Nelson, New Zealand, where it forms a prostrate, evergreen subshrub only a few inches tall with glossy, leathery, deeply divided foliage, a sharp contrast to the large vining clematis most gardeners know. In early spring it opens small, creamy-white, star-like flowers under an inch across, sometimes tinged green. Because it is only half-hardy and resents winter wet, grow it in a container that can be moved under cover or into an unheated greenhouse where winters are cold and damp.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, giving the vine a trellis, obelisk or shrub to scramble through in full sun.

directions: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, giving the vine a trellis, obelisk or shrub to scramble through in full sun. Native to Portugal and western and southern Spain, Clematis campaniflora is a close relative of C. viticella but is distinguished by narrower, more deeply bell-shaped, nodding flowers held singly or in small clusters, blooming pale violet-white from midsummer into early fall. Like other viticella-group clematis, it flowers entirely on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter without sacrificing bloom. In cultivation in Europe since at least the early 1800s, it offers an airy, small-flowered alternative to bolder large-flowered hybrid clematis.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
